newsitem.title: GERMANY: German govt searches for budget, tax compromise.
newsitem.headline: German govt searches for budget, tax compromise.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right government struggled in vain on Tuesday to end a smouldering feud on tax reform and the 1997 budget that has badly strained his record 14-year coalition.

His Christian Democrats (CDU), Bavaria CSU allies and Free Democrat (FDP) partners failed to find several billion marks to ensure the 1997 budget does not overstep the strict Maastricht criteria on new government debt, officials said.
The coalition partners, under pressure to find a compromise in the coming weeks, planned another meeting later on Tuesday to continue their search for a compromise.
Kohl, who returned at the weekend from a Far Eastern tour, upbraided the FDP on Monday for attacking Finance Minister Theo Waigel and threw his weight behind the embattled CSU chairman.
But leading Free Democrats kept up their pressure on Waigel, who last month tarnished their image as a tax-cutting party by forcing them to agree to put off a promised tax cut.
"The problem for the coalition is Theo Waigel," FDP deputy Juergen Koppelin said. "He is a danger for the coalition."

Former Economics Minister Juergen Moellemann, the target of Kohl's sharp words on Monday, warned FDP deputies might vote against the budget if Waigel did not agree now to reduce the hated "solidarity tax" for east Germany by two points in 1998.
Kohl and Waigel do not want to commit themselves to future tax cuts before they know whether they can afford them.
The budget dispute has highlighted that Germany, which has led the campaign for a rock-solid single European currency, now finds itself hemmed in by the strict guidelines it supports.

The FDP has been piling the pressure on Waigel because it fears the official tax revenue estimate due on Friday will show he should have up to 10 billion marks less to work with in 1997 than his ministry has assumed until now.
The FDP threatened to pull out of the coalition last month when Waigel said he would need to raise gasoline taxes to make up for unforeseen extra costs in 1997.
Agreeing to delay a cut in the "solidarity tax" was a bitter pill for the struggling FDP, which has little more than its tax-cutting image to appeal to voters.
Waigel said in an interview with Stern magazine he might be able to agree to the two percent cut in the "solidarity tax" if this can be fit into a larger tax reform package Bonn is planning for 1999.
He assured the FDP he would not raise taxes next year and that the defence ministry would not be exempted from any across-the-board spending cuts ministries might have to make.
